questions.q: Fire needs three things together to keep burning. These are:
options: Heat, smoke and light
Fuel, water and oxygen
Heat, fuel and oxygen — removing any one extinguishes the fire
Heat, fuel and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: This is the fire triangle — every extinguishing method works by removing heat, fuel or oxygen.

questions.q: In the commonly used Indian training classification, a fire involving live electrical equipment is class:
options: Class E
Class A
Class B
Class D
questions.explain: Class A is solids, B liquids, C gases, D metals — and E is the electrical class used in Indian training.

questions.q: A fire in a heap of wooden sleepers and packing material is a class:
options: Class B — liquids
Class C — gases
Class E — electrical
Class A — solid materials
questions.explain: Wood, paper and cloth are ordinary solids — Class A fires.

questions.q: A petrol or oil fire belongs to class:
options: Class A — solids
Class B — flammable liquids
Class C — gases
Class D — metals
questions.explain: Liquids like petrol and oil are Class B — they spread if fought wrongly, so the extinguisher choice matters.

questions.q: For a fire on live electrical equipment, the correct extinguishers are:
options: CO2 or dry powder
Water jet
Foam only
Sand and water together
questions.explain: CO2 and dry powder do not conduct electricity — they are the safe choice on live equipment.

questions.q: Water must never be used on a live electrical fire because:
options: Water makes the fire burn brighter
Water is too costly to waste
Water conducts electricity and can electrocute the person using it
Water damages the paint of equipment
questions.explain: The jet becomes a live conductor back to the user's hands — a classic exam trap.

questions.q: Fire is reported on a train standing at a station platform. The correct action is:
options: Depart immediately to clear the station
Keep the train there, open the doors and evacuate passengers onto the platform
Close the doors and wait inside
Drive the train into the tunnel to isolate it
questions.explain: A train already at a station is already at the safest evacuation place — use it.

questions.q: Fire is reported on a moving train inside a tunnel, and the train can still move. The best action is:
options: Stop at once and evacuate inside the tunnel
Open all doors while the train is moving
Reverse back through the tunnel against the traffic direction
Drive the train to the nearest station and evacuate there
questions.explain: A burning train stopped in a tunnel is the worst case — the station gives light, space, staff and ambulances.

questions.q: A burning train in a tunnel genuinely cannot move. The priority becomes:
options: Wait in the tunnel until the fire burns itself out
Send passengers out in all directions to find exits
Continue normal service on the other line at full speed
Inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), protect and evacuate passengers under control towards fresh air, with ventilation set correctly
questions.explain: If the train cannot reach the station, controlled evacuation against the smoke flow is the fallback.

questions.q: In a station fire, the ventilation system should be set to:
options: Normal comfort mode
Smoke-extraction mode, pushing smoke away from the evacuation routes
Off, to save power
Supply mode blowing air towards the fire and the exits together
questions.explain: Passengers must walk in fresh air — ventilation protects the escape route, not the fire.

questions.q: During a fire evacuation, passengers should move:
options: Against the smoke flow, towards fresh air
With the smoke flow, as it is faster
Towards the nearest train
Into the tunnel to escape the station
questions.explain: Smoke kills faster than flame — moving against its flow leads to breathable air.

questions.q: Why must lifts not be used during a fire evacuation?
options: Lifts are reserved for staff during fires
Lifts are too slow for large crowds
A lift can fail, trap people, or open onto the fire floor
Lift lobbies are locked during all emergencies
questions.explain: Stairs are the fire exit; a lift shaft can fill with smoke and the car can stop at the fire level.

questions.q: Escalators during a station fire evacuation are:
options: Run at double speed
Stopped or used as stairs, as directed by staff
Reserved for passengers with luggage
Switched off and barricaded permanently
questions.explain: A stopped escalator is simply a staircase — used as directed, never as a moving crowd machine.

questions.q: A small fire has just started in an electrical cabinet and a trained staff member is present. He should:
options: Attack it at once with a CO2 or dry powder extinguisher, if it is safe to do so
Pour a bucket of water over it
Wait for the fire brigade before doing anything
Open the cabinet and fan the flames out
questions.explain: Small, early fires are the only ones staff fight — with the correct extinguisher and a safe escape behind them.

questions.q: Staff should attempt to fight a fire themselves only when:
options: The fire has spread to two rooms
Passengers ask them to try
It is small and early, they are trained, have the right extinguisher and a safe exit
The fire brigade is delayed by an hour
questions.explain: Beyond the small-and-early stage, the job is evacuation and handover, not firefighting.

questions.q: On discovering a fire, the first information Operations Control Centre (OCC)/station control needs is:
options: The name of the person who saw it first
The cost of equipment nearby
The train's catering details
The exact location of the fire
questions.explain: Location decides everything — response, ventilation mode, evacuation route and brigade access.

questions.q: When fire services arrive at a station, staff hand over with a brief covering:
options: Location of the fire, electrical status, and any casualties
The day's ticket collection figures
The station's cleaning schedule
Names of all staff on leave
questions.explain: One clear brief — where it is, whether power is live, and who is hurt — lets the brigade start work at once.

questions.q: During a fire evacuation, traction power of the affected section may need to be isolated when:
options: Passengers complain about the lights
People may contact electrical equipment, or fire services need to use water
The fire is in another city
The timetable is running late
questions.explain: Isolation protects evacuees and firefighters — especially before water is used anywhere near equipment.

questions.q: A staff member is assigned to meet the fire brigade. Where should he wait?
options: Inside the station control room
At the station entrance of his choice
At the designated access point, to guide them straight to the site
At the depot, by phone
questions.explain: Minutes saved in guiding the brigade in are worth more than extra equipment waiting outside.

questions.q: Smoke is spreading in an underground station but no flames are visible. The correct approach is:
options: Treat it as a fire emergency — ventilate, evacuate and investigate under control
Ignore it until flames appear
Open all platform screen doors and continue service
Announce that it is only a technical fault and do nothing
questions.explain: Smoke without flame still kills and still signals fire somewhere — it is never ignored.

questions.q: The fire alarm in a station should trigger, among other things:
options: Automatic cancellation of all tickets
Music to keep passengers calm
Closure of all exits to contain the smoke
Clear Public Address (PA) announcements telling passengers what happened, where to go and what not to do
questions.explain: Announcements direct the evacuation — what happened, where to go, and no lifts.

questions.q: After a station fire evacuation, who can declare the all-clear for people to re-enter?
options: Any passenger who sees no smoke
The first staff member to return
Only the authorised command, after the area is checked and accounted for
The train operator of the next service
questions.explain: Re-entry on assumption is how people walk back into danger — the all-clear is a formal decision.

questions.q: Passengers are evacuating from a smoky platform. A man heads back towards the smoke to collect his bag. Staff should:
options: Let him go as the bag is his property
Stop him and direct him to the assembly point — belongings are never worth a life
Ask another passenger to fetch it
Escort a group back for everyone's luggage
questions.explain: Returning into smoke for property is a classic cause of fire deaths — staff prevent it firmly.

questions.q: Which extinguisher-related pairing is correct?
options: Electrical fire — CO2 extinguisher
Electrical fire — water extinguisher
Petrol fire — water jet
Metal fire — foam only
questions.explain: Match the medium to the class: CO2/dry powder for electrical is the pairing examiners test most.

questions.q: In a tunnel fire, the ventilation direction is chosen so that:
options: Smoke is pushed over the evacuees to speed them up
Air is stopped completely in the tunnel
Smoke collects at the evacuation route
Evacuees walk into fresh air while smoke is pushed away from them
questions.explain: Ventilation is a life-safety system here — it defends the walking route.

questions.q: A train operator smells burning inside his train at a station. His first two actions are:
options: Depart quickly to clear the platform
Raise the alarm and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), keeping the train at the station
Investigate alone for ten minutes first
Ask passengers to check under their seats
questions.explain: Alarm plus information starts the whole response; departing would carry a possible fire into the tunnel.

questions.q: Why is a fire in a train standing in a tunnel considered the worst case?
options: Tunnels have no mobile signal for passengers
The train cannot be cleaned there
Smoke and heat are trapped, exits are far, and help cannot reach quickly
Passengers cannot buy refreshments
questions.explain: Confined smoke, distance from exits and difficult access combine — hence the rule to reach a station.

questions.q: During evacuation for fire, the assembly point is used to:
options: Gather everyone and take a headcount to confirm nobody is missing
Sell refreshments to evacuated passengers
Park the rescue vehicles
Hold a press conference
questions.explain: Assembly plus headcount is how 'everyone out' is proved, not assumed.

questions.q: A fire is reported in a closed room at a station and the door feels hot. The staff member should:
options: Open it quickly to look inside
Not open it; inform control, evacuate the area and let fire services handle it
Pour water under the door and open it
Send a passenger to check
questions.explain: A hot door means a developed fire behind it — opening feeds it air and endangers the opener.

questions.q: What is the correct order in a station fire response?
options: Restore, evacuate, report, ventilate, call fire services
Call press, evacuate, detect, fight, report
Fight the fire first in all cases, report afterwards
Detect and report, ventilate, evacuate, call fire services, fight small fires only, then account and restore
questions.explain: Detection and information start the chain; restoration comes only after accounting and certification.

questions.q: If smoke enters a train standing at a platform from a station fire, the operator should:
options: Follow Operations Control Centre (OCC)/station instructions — detrain passengers away from the smoke as directed
Close doors and keep passengers inside indefinitely
Depart into the tunnel without instruction
Open doors on the smoke side only
questions.explain: The train becomes part of the station evacuation — movements follow the incident command, not habit.

questions.q: Fire services ask whether the section's power is isolated. This information matters to them because:
options: It decides their vehicle's parking place
It changes the colour of the smoke
It decides whether they can safely use water and approach equipment
It is needed for their attendance register
questions.explain: Electrical status is a life-safety fact for firefighters — it is always in the handover brief.

questions.q: A small dustbin fire on a platform is noticed early. The proportionate response is:
options: Evacuate the whole city station network
Close the station for the full day automatically
Ignore it as too small to matter
Extinguish it with the correct extinguisher, inform station control, and watch the area
questions.explain: Small fires are fought early and reported — neither ignored nor inflated into a network closure.

questions.q: Why are fire exits and emergency gates opened during a station evacuation?
options: To let fresh passengers enter faster
To give the crowd several wide, quick routes out instead of one narrow flow
To cool the station with outside air
To allow shops to close early
questions.explain: Exit capacity decides evacuation time — every opened gate relieves the crowd.

questions.q: After a fire incident ends, trains may resume only after:
options: Inspection and certification that the area and systems are safe
The smoke smell has faded
Passengers have stopped complaining
One hour has passed since the fire
questions.explain: Resumption is gated by a 'declared fit' — never by the clock or by smell.

questions.q: The correct technique for using a portable fire extinguisher is remembered as PASS. It stands for:
options: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side
Push, Alarm, Shout, Sprinkle
Pick, Aim, Spray, Stop
Pull, Aim, Spray at the flames' top, Shake
questions.explain: Pull, Aim (at the base, where the fuel is), Squeeze, Sweep — the PASS sequence is the standard first-aid firefighting method taught across Indian Railways and metro systems.

questions.q: A Manual Call Point (the red break-glass unit) on a station wall is used to:
options: Open the fare gates
Manually raise the fire alarm at once when a person discovers a fire, without waiting for automatic detectors
Call the station master's office telephone
Stop an escalator
questions.explain: Detectors react to smoke or heat; a Manual Call Point lets a human raise the alarm the second a fire is seen. Breaking the glass sets off the station fire alarm sequence.

questions.q: During a station fire, ordinary lifts must not be used by passengers — but a designated fire lift is different because it is:
options: Faster than other lifts
Reserved for the fire services, with protected shaft and power supply, so firefighters can reach upper or lower levels under their control
Used by staff to save their belongings
Open to passengers who have a special ticket
questions.explain: The 'no lifts in fire' rule is for public lifts, which may fail or open onto smoke. A fire lift is a protected tool of the fire brigade — passengers still use stairs and ramps.

questions.q: A fire involving reactive metals such as magnesium (Class D) needs special care because:
options: It is not really a fire
Water and ordinary extinguishers can react violently with burning metal; only special dry powder meant for metal fires should be used
It goes out on its own in seconds
It can be blown out by fanning
questions.explain: Class D metal fires are a specialist case: the wrong agent makes them worse. Isolate the area, inform the Operations Control Centre (OCC) and leave metal fires to the fire services with the correct powder.

questions.q: In a smoke-filled area, the safest way for a person to move towards an exit is to:
options: Run upright as fast as possible through the smoke
Stay low — crouch or crawl — because hot smoke and toxic gases rise and the cleaner air is near the floor
Hold their breath and walk backwards
Wait in the middle of the room until the smoke clears
questions.explain: Smoke kills more people than flames. Hot smoke layers at the ceiling, so the breathable air is low — stay low, cover nose and mouth if possible, and move to fresh air.
